headline: Research shows that "jurisdiction" decides whose human rights a state must protect
dek: A 2012 legal study argues that the concept of "jurisdiction" — often poorly defined — is the critical but underexamined threshold that determines when a state owes human rights duties to people beyond its own borders under the European Convention on Human Rights.
summary_md:
## What they found

When does a government have to respect *your* human rights if you're not even in its country? According to this study, the answer hinges almost entirely on a single, surprisingly slippery word: **jurisdiction**.

The paper argues that human rights law — and specifically the European Court of Human Rights' case law — has generated a rich body of practice on "extraterritoriality" (applying rights protections outside a state's own territory), but that the underlying reasoning has been left frustratingly vague. Courts and scholars have often leaned on broad appeals to the *universality* of human rights as a justification, without actually working out the normative logic: **why** does a state owe duties to a foreigner abroad, and precisely **when** do those duties kick in?

The author's central move is to treat "jurisdiction" not as a bureaucratic formality but as a **morally loaded threshold concept** — the trigger that determines when abstract human rights translate into concrete state obligations. Crucially, the paper distinguishes jurisdiction from related but distinct ideas: authority, coercion, power, and control. These terms are often used interchangeably in legal discourse, but the article argues they are not the same thing, and conflating them produces confused and inconsistent outcomes in human rights adjudication.

## How they studied it

This is a work of **legal and normative theory**, not an empirical study. The author reviews the European Court of Human Rights' recent case law on extraterritorial applicability of the ECHR, identifies gaps between legal practice and its theoretical justification, and then draws on human rights theory — particularly perspectives that take seriously the "supply side" of human rights (i.e., who bears the duty to fulfil them) — to build a more coherent account of what jurisdiction should mean and what normative consequences follow from it.

The method is analytical and philosophical: close reading of case law combined with engagement with human rights scholarship that has, the author contends, largely neglected these threshold questions.

## Caveats & limits

- This is a **theoretical and doctrinal argument**, not an empirical measurement of outcomes. It does not test whether courts have actually adopted or benefited from cleaner jurisdiction concepts.
- The analysis is focused on the **European Convention on Human Rights** and the European Court; conclusions may not transfer directly to other regional or UN human rights systems.
- The abstract does not specify which particular cases or states are examined in depth, so the empirical breadth of the case law review is unclear.
- The paper dates to **2012**, and the Court's extraterritoriality jurisprudence has continued to evolve since then.

## Why it matters

This kind of quiet conceptual work has real-world stakes. When a state's military operates abroad, when its border agents turn back migrants at sea, or when its surveillance programs reach foreign nationals — the question of whether human rights protections apply turns directly on how "jurisdiction" is defined. **Vague concepts produce inconsistent rulings**, which means people in identical situations may receive different legal protections depending on which judge interprets the word. By pushing for a sharper, normatively grounded definition, the paper argues for a more principled — and more predictable — human rights law.
talking_point: Turns out whether your human rights are protected by a foreign government — say, during a military operation or a border interception — comes down to one vague legal word: "jurisdiction."

paper.title: The Extraterritoriality of the European Convention on Human Rights: Why Human Rights Depend on Jurisdiction and What Jurisdiction Amounts to
